script.opening: "Right, I’ll not waste your time — I know the drink’s out of hand and I’m done with it. I’ve decided: Monday, that’s it, I’m stopping dead, no more. I just wanted to tell someone official so it’s real. I don’t need rehab or any of that, I’ve got the willpower this time. So really I’m just letting you know — unless there’s a tablet that helps with the willpower?"

facts.text: If explored: drinks first thing to stop the shakes (relief drinking), morning sweats/tremor, anxiety, has had a "fit" once years ago during a previous attempt to stop suddenly. This is physical alcohol dependence — abrupt unplanned cessation risks withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens.

HIDDEN AGENDA / red flag — reachable with direct questioning: twice this week he vomited "coffee-ground" / some bright blood, and his stools have been "black and sticky". He’s terrified this means cancer or that he’s "dying inside", so he’s told no one and is minimising it. This is a possible variceal/upper-GI bleed — an EMERGENCY hiding under the "cutting down" agenda.

If asked/observed: yellow tinge, ankle swelling, abdomen "bloated", more forgetful/muddled this week (his partner says he’s "vague"). Possible decompensated liver disease (jaundice, ascites, early encephalopathy).

If reached gently: the "Monday, on my own" plan is partly bravado over fear; he’s frightened, ashamed, his partner has threatened to leave, and there’s a flicker of "everyone’d be better off" — needs a sensitive risk/mood screen.

Officially: to announce he’s quitting and maybe get a "willpower tablet". Actually: to be made safe — he is closer to a withdrawal seizure and a serious bleed than he realises — and to be met with help, not judgement, for a problem that frightens him.

ice.ideas: Willpower is all he needs; stopping abruptly on his own on Monday is the responsible plan; maybe a tablet helps.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a concealed upper-GI bleed (coffee-ground vomit, melaena) he’s hiding from fear it’s cancer/dying; plus shame, a relationship in crisis, and a flicker of hopelessness.
ice.expectations: To be told to go ahead and stop. What he actually needs: recognition that abrupt cessation is dangerous in dependence, urgent assessment of a possible bleed and decompensation, and compassionate help with detox and mood.

cues: "I’m stopping dead, on my own, Monday" — in physical dependence this is dangerous, not admirable; do not simply praise it.
Morning shakes relieved by drinking + a past "fit" — physical dependence with seizure risk.
"Black sticky stools / brought up some blood" mentioned almost as an aside — the emergency hiding under the stated agenda.

checkpoints.text: Identifies the concealed upper-GI bleed as an EMERGENCY: coffee-ground/fresh haematemesis + melaena in a likely-cirrhotic drinker suggests variceal or other upper-GI bleeding — arranges immediate emergency admission by ambulance (999/acute medical/upper-GI), not a routine plan — in hospital, risk scoring, terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics for suspected variceal bleeding, and endoscopy within 24 hours or immediately after resuscitation if unstable (NICE CG141; BSG 2015)

Recognises physical alcohol DEPENDENCE and the danger of abrupt unplanned cessation: relief drinking, morning tremor/sweats, prior withdrawal seizure → abrupt stopping risks seizures and delirium tremens; does NOT simply endorse "stopping dead on Monday on his own"
Assesses for decompensated liver disease and encephalopathy: jaundice, ascites/abdominal swelling, ankle oedema, confusion/vagueness — and factors these into urgency and admission

Explains safe alcohol withdrawal management: medically-supported detox (community or inpatient depending on risk — NICE CG100 and CG115: inpatient given the withdrawal seizure history and chronic liver disease, let alone the bleed), the role of benzodiazepine regimens and thiamine (Pabrinex/oral) to prevent Wernicke’s — rather than a "willpower tablet"

Carries out a sensitive risk/mood assessment: shame, relationship breakdown, hopelessness and any suicidal ideation — and responds appropriately to the flicker of "everyone’d be better off" (NICE NG225)

Reframes "stopping on my own" without crushing his motivation: harnesses the readiness to change while making clear that doing it safely, with support, is what protects him — turning bravado into a real, supported plan
Responds to the concealed bleed and the fear behind it (cancer/dying) with calm seriousness and compassion, so he accepts urgent care rather than fleeing it

Acts on the emergency now and scaffolds the rest: immediate admission for the bleed/decompensation, thiamine, alcohol-team/detox referral, mood/safeguarding follow-up, and partner/social support — a coordinated plan, not a leaflet

worked.txt: "Sean, before anything else — you mentioned bringing up something dark and your stools going black and sticky. I need to stop you there, because that can mean bleeding inside, and with your liver that’s something we treat as an emergency today, not Monday. I’m really glad you said it, even in passing. Tell me exactly how much and when."

"I can hear how ready you are to stop, and that genuinely matters — but I have to be honest with you, because it could save your life: when someone’s body is as used to alcohol as yours is, stopping dead on your own can cause fits and a dangerous confused state. You’ve even had a fit before stopping suddenly. So we don’t cancel your plan — we make it SAFE, with support and medication, so it actually works and doesn’t harm you."

"Can I check a few things — the yellow tinge, your tummy feeling bloated, your ankles, and your partner saying you’ve been a bit vague this week? Those tell me your liver’s under real strain right now, which is another reason today needs to be about getting you assessed properly, not waiting."

"There isn’t a ‘willpower tablet’ — and the fact you need a drink in the morning to stop the shakes isn’t weak willpower, it’s your body being physically dependent, which is a medical thing we treat. Safe stopping uses medication to cover the withdrawal and vitamin B1 to protect your brain. Done right, with the alcohol team, you get through the dangerous bit and out the other side."

"This sounds like it’s been a brutal few months — off work, things hard at home. When people are this low, sometimes the thought comes that everyone’d be better off without them. Has anything like that crossed your mind? … Thank you for telling me. You’re not a burden, and you’re not doing this alone from here."

"So here’s what happens now: because of the bleeding and how your liver’s doing, I’m arranging for you to be seen in hospital today — that’s the urgent bit. They’ll keep you safe through stopping the alcohol too, with the right medication and vitamins. I’ll link you with the alcohol team and make sure your mood and your home situation are part of the plan. You came in to tell someone you’re done with the drink — and I’m going to make sure that decision doesn’t cost you your life on the way."

f.learning: "I want to cut down" can conceal two emergencies. First, the hidden red flag: coffee-ground/fresh haematemesis and melaena in a likely-cirrhotic drinker is a possible variceal bleed — an immediate admission, not a routine plan; it hides here because the patient is terrified it means cancer. Second, the danger in his stated plan: physical alcohol dependence (relief drinking, morning tremor, a prior withdrawal seizure) makes abrupt unplanned cessation hazardous — seizures and delirium tremens — so "stopping dead on Monday on my own" must be redirected to medically-supported detox with benzodiazepines and thiamine (Wernicke’s prevention; NICE CG100 and CG115 — inpatient here), not praised. The bleed itself is managed per NICE CG141 (acute upper GI bleeding), not as a cancer-referral question. Add assessment for decompensation (jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy) and a sensitive risk/mood screen (shame, relationship crisis, hopelessness). The skill is to catch the bleed, refuse to endorse unsafe self-detox without crushing motivation, act on the emergency today, and wrap the patient in coordinated, compassionate care.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG141 · NICE CG100 · NICE CG115 · NICE NG50 · BSG variceal haemorrhage guideline (2015) · NICE NG225 · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
knowledge.summary: Haematemesis and melaena in a heavy drinker with probable cirrhosis is a possible variceal bleed and needs emergency admission today. In physical dependence with a previous withdrawal seizure, abrupt unsupported stopping is dangerous; withdrawal must be medically managed.

points.t: Coffee-ground or fresh haematemesis with black, tarry stools means upper GI bleeding. Low platelets, raised MCV and deranged LFTs in a heavy drinker suggest cirrhosis and portal hypertension, so varices are likely. Arrange emergency admission by ambulance. In hospital: risk scoring, terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics for suspected variceal bleeding, and endoscopy within 24 hours, or immediately after resuscitation if unstable (NICE CG141; BSG 2015).

Relief drinking for morning shakes and sweats, rising tolerance and a previous withdrawal seizure mean physical dependence. NICE CG100: offer hospital admission for medically assisted withdrawal to people in acute withdrawal, or at high risk of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens.

NICE CG115: consider inpatient or residential assisted withdrawal for a SADQ score above 30, a history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, or significant physical comorbidity such as chronic liver disease. Sean meets more than one criterion; community detox would be unsafe.

Benzodiazepine regimen for withdrawal, chosen and dosed by the treating team with his liver function in mind (dose per BNF). NICE CG100: thiamine for people at high risk of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, including those with decompensated liver disease or in acute withdrawal; parenteral at the upper end of the BNF range if Wernicke’s is suspected. There is no tablet for willpower; relapse-prevention drugs come after withdrawal.

Jaundice, abdominal swelling (ascites), ankle oedema and new vagueness or confusion (hepatic encephalopathy) suggest decompensated cirrhosis. With a bleed, encephalopathy can worsen quickly. After recovery, NICE NG50 covers cirrhosis assessment and surveillance.

Alcohol dependence carries a high suicide risk. Ask directly about hopelessness and thoughts of suicide, and respond to what he says (NICE NG225). Shame, a threatened break-up and 3 months off work are all risk factors.

Off work 3 months, partner threatening to leave, shame, who is at home today.
Postural symptoms asked on video; hospital assessment, bloods and endoscopy arranged through admission.
Variceal vs peptic bleed; decompensated cirrhosis; withdrawal risk; mood disorder.
Recognised a probable upper GI bleed, decompensation and encephalopathy; asked directly about suicidal thoughts.
Probable variceal bleed with decompensated alcohol-related liver disease and physical dependence, in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Mood and suicide risk followed up; alcohol service after discharge; partner involved with consent.
999 triggers while waiting; crisis numbers; GP phone call after discharge.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (willpower and stopping Monday), concern (cancer, dying), expectation (a willpower tablet).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — a concealed upper-GI bleed (coffee-ground vomit, melaena) he’s hiding from fear it’s cancer/dying; plus shame, a relationship in crisis, and a flicker of hopelessness — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Sean, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for booking in. It takes guts to ask about drink. Tell me where things are at.
model.why: Validates the step of asking for help and opens

model.text: I’ll not waste your time. The drink’s out of hand. Monday, I’m stopping dead, on my own. I just wanted to tell someone official. Unless there’s a tablet for willpower?

I’m really glad you want to stop, and I want to help you do it. So that we make a plan that works, can I ask some questions about the drinking and how your body is doing? You don’t look well to me today, and I’d like to understand why.
model.why: Supports his motivation while setting an agenda that includes his physical state

model.text: Aye, fair enough.
Walk me through a normal day’s drinking. When’s the first drink?
model.why: Quantifies drinking and screens for relief drinking

model.text: First thing, to stop the shakes. Half a bottle of vodka over the day, and cans. This morning I was shaking and sweating till I had one.
Have you tried stopping before? What happened?
Couple of years back. I had a fit on day two. Ended up in A&E.
Thank you, that’s very important. I’ll come back to it. How has your body been lately? Any vomiting, and any change in your stools?
I brought up some dark stuff twice this week. Bit of red in it. And my poo’s gone black and sticky. It’s probably nothing.

Sean, I’m going to stop you there, because that matters more than anything else today. Dark vomit with blood and black, sticky stools can mean bleeding inside. When was the last time, and do you feel faint or dizzy when you stand?
model.why: Recognises the red flag and assesses current severity

model.text: Last night. Not dizzy, just washed out.
Have you noticed your eyes going yellow, your tummy swelling, or your ankles? And has anyone said you’ve seemed muddled?
model.why: Screens for decompensated liver disease and encephalopathy

model.text: The yellow, yeah. Tummy’s bloated, ankles are puffy. My partner says I’ve been vague this week.
You called the bleeding ‘probably nothing’, but you mentioned it. What have you been thinking it might be?
model.why: Explores the fear behind the concealment

model.text: Cancer. Or that I’m dying inside. That’s why I’ve not told anyone. If I stop drinking, maybe it goes away.

That’s a frightening thing to carry on your own. Things sound hard at home too. When people are this low, sometimes they think everyone would be better off without them. Has anything like that crossed your mind?
Now and then. I wouldn’t do anything. I’ve not got a plan. It’s just a thought when I’m low.
Thank you for being honest. That thought is common when things are this bad, and we’ll take it seriously and get you support. You’re not a burden.
model.why: Responds with compassion and commits to follow it up

model.text: I’ll be straight with you, because it could save your life. The black stools and the blood mean you may be bleeding from swollen veins in your gullet, which happens when the liver is scarred. That needs hospital today. Not Monday: now.
model.why: Explains the probable variceal bleed and the urgency plainly

model.text: Today? I can’t just…

I know it’s a shock. It can be treated, but it has to be done in hospital. The yellow, the swelling and being vague tell me your liver is struggling too. Is it cancer? I can’t say yet, but bleeding like this in someone who drinks heavily is much more often from those veins, and that’s treatable.
model.why: Answers the cancer fear honestly without false reassurance

model.text: Right.

And about Monday: your wish to stop is exactly right. But with your body this used to alcohol, and a fit last time, stopping dead on your own could cause another fit or a dangerous confused state. We don’t cancel your plan; we make it safe. In hospital they’ll cover the withdrawal with medication and give you vitamin B1 to protect your brain.
model.why: Refuses to endorse unsafe self-detox while keeping his motivation

model.text: Here’s what I’d like to do now. I’m going to call an ambulance while we’re on this call. Is someone with you? Please don’t drive, and don’t have any more to drink or eat for now.
model.why: Immediate action: ambulance, checks he is not alone, practical instructions

model.text: My partner’s downstairs. Okay. I’ll go.

Thank you. That’s the brave choice. Can you put her on for a moment so she knows what to watch for until they arrive? I’ll also write to the hospital today, and once you’re out I’ll link you with the alcohol service for support to stay stopped.
model.why: Involves the partner with consent and coordinates care beyond discharge

model.text: Aye. She’ll be relieved, to be honest.

I’ll make sure your mood is part of the plan too. I’ll phone you after discharge. If the low thoughts get stronger at any point, tell the ward staff, or ring 111 option 2 or the Samaritans on 116 123.
model.why: Builds the mood follow-up and crisis contacts into the plan

model.text: While you wait, if you vomit more blood, feel faint, become more confused or have a fit, your partner should ring 999 again and tell them. Lie on your side if you feel faint.
model.why: Specific safety-net for the minutes before the ambulance

model.text: Got it.
Just so I know we’re on the same page, what’s happening next?
Ambulance, hospital for the bleeding, and they’ll help me come off the drink safely. Not doing it on my own Monday.
Exactly. You came to tell someone you’re done with drink. I’m going to make sure you get through it safely.

social.t: Partner threatening to leave and 3 months off work. Involve his partner with consent; she is also the person who can call for help. Fit note and benefits advice after discharge.
Shame drives concealment of the bleed and delays help. A non-judgemental stance is what gets him into the ambulance.

legal.t: Alcohol dependence is a notifiable condition for drivers. With high-risk features (his previous withdrawal seizure; medication-assisted withdrawal): licence refused or revoked until at least 1 year (Group 1) or 3 years (Group 2) of abstinence (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive). If he drives, advise him of his duty to tell DVLA; GMC Confidentiality 2017 sets out what to do if he continues to drive against advice.
If he became confused and refused admission, assess capacity for that decision under the Mental Capacity Act 2005; encephalopathy can impair it. Act in his best interests if he lacks capacity.

professional.t: Supporting his autonomy does not mean endorsing an unsafe plan. Explain the risk clearly and document the advice and his decision (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Phone the admitting team, send a summary including the previous withdrawal seizure and suicidal thoughts, and follow up after discharge.

community.t: Local community alcohol service after discharge; mutual-aid groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous or SMART Recovery; Al-Anon for his partner; Samaritans 116 123 and NHS 111 option 2 for mental health crisis.

Jaundice, ascites, oedema and new confusion: decompensated liver disease and possible encephalopathy
Suicidal thoughts in the context of dependence, shame and relationship crisis
psychosocial: Partner threatening to leave; who is at home now
Off work 3 months; money and identity

playbook.diagnosis: Probable acute upper GI bleed, likely variceal, with decompensated alcohol-related liver disease (jaundice, ascites, oedema, possible early encephalopathy) in a man with physical alcohol dependence and a previous withdrawal seizure; passive suicidal thoughts without a plan.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The black stools and the blood mean you’re probably bleeding from swollen veins in your gullet, which happens when drink has scarred the liver. That needs treating in hospital today. And because your body depends on alcohol, stopping suddenly on your own could cause a fit, so the hospital will help you stop safely.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been hiding the bleeding because you were scared it meant cancer. Telling me was the right thing, and it’s treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Involve his partner with consent; mood and suicide risk followed up; alcohol service and fit note after discharge.
sharedPlan: Ambulance now for probable upper GI bleed (NICE CG141); do not drive, nothing further to drink
Medically assisted withdrawal with benzodiazepines and thiamine in hospital (NICE CG100; NICE CG115)
Community alcohol service, cirrhosis follow-up (NICE NG50) and mood support after discharge
safetyNet: Partner to call 999 again for more blood, fainting, worsening confusion or a fit before the ambulance arrives
Crisis numbers for suicidal thoughts; GP phone call after discharge

pitfalls.intro: This station hides two emergencies under a request that sounds routine. It is failed by the candidate who praises the plan, misses the bleed, and ends with a leaflet.

items.fail: Missing the haematemesis and melaena because he mentions them as an aside, or never asking.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” A probable variceal bleed needs admission today (NICE CG141).
items.fix: Ask every heavy drinker: “Any vomiting of blood or dark material? Have your stools gone black or sticky?”

items.fail: Endorsing ‘stopping dead on Monday’ as a positive step.
items.why: With a previous withdrawal seizure he is at high risk of seizures and delirium tremens; NICE CG100 advises admission for medically assisted withdrawal.
items.fix: Welcome the decision, redirect the method: “We don’t cancel your plan; we make it safe.”

items.why: NICE CG115 criteria for inpatient withdrawal are met: previous withdrawal seizure and chronic liver disease, before even counting the bleed.
items.fix: State that withdrawal will be managed in hospital, with thiamine.

items.fail: Delivering the emergency coldly, so he refuses to go.
items.why: His fear of cancer is why he concealed it; a blunt order can make him disengage.
items.fix: Answer the fear honestly: bleeding like this is more often from treatable veins than cancer, and hospital is how it gets treated.

items.why: Dependence, shame and a relationship crisis raise suicide risk; omitting the question is unsafe (NICE NG225).
items.fix: Ask directly and kindly, then build mood follow-up and crisis numbers into the plan.

items.fail: Telling him to get himself to A&E and ending the call.
items.why: He may still be bleeding and may be encephalopathic; he may drive, or not go at all.
items.fix: Call the ambulance during the consultation, check who is with him, brief his partner and phone the admitting team.

avoid.instead: “Your decision to stop is exactly right. Doing it suddenly on your own could cause a fit, so let’s make it safe.”
avoid.why: Endorsing unsupported withdrawal after a previous seizure is a patient-safety fail.

I know it’s a shock. It can be treated, but it has to be done in hospital. The yellow, the swelling and being vague tell me your liver is struggling too. Is it cancer? I can’t say yet, but bleeding like this in someone who drinks heavily is much more often from those veins, and that’s treatable.
SCA_MODELS.why: Answers the cancer fear honestly without false reassurance

SCA_MODELS.text: Right.

And about Monday: your wish to stop is exactly right. But with your body this used to alcohol, and a fit last time, stopping dead on your own could cause another fit or a dangerous confused state. We don’t cancel your plan; we make it safe. In hospital they’ll cover the withdrawal with medication and give you vitamin B1 to protect your brain.
SCA_MODELS.why: Refuses to endorse unsafe self-detox while keeping his motivation

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s what I’d like to do now. I’m going to call an ambulance while we’re on this call. Is someone with you? Please don’t drive, and don’t have any more to drink or eat for now.
SCA_MODELS.why: Immediate action: ambulance, checks he is not alone, practical instructions

SCA_MODELS.text: My partner’s downstairs. Okay. I’ll go.

Thank you. That’s the brave choice. Can you put her on for a moment so she knows what to watch for until they arrive? I’ll also write to the hospital today, and once you’re out I’ll link you with the alcohol service for support to stay stopped.
SCA_MODELS.why: Involves the partner with consent and coordinates care beyond discharge

SCA_MODELS.text: Aye. She’ll be relieved, to be honest.

I’ll make sure your mood is part of the plan too. I’ll phone you after discharge. If the low thoughts get stronger at any point, tell the ward staff, or ring 111 option 2 or the Samaritans on 116 123.
SCA_MODELS.why: Builds the mood follow-up and crisis contacts into the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: While you wait, if you vomit more blood, feel faint, become more confused or have a fit, your partner should ring 999 again and tell them. Lie on your side if you feel faint.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net for the minutes before the ambulance

SCA_MODELS.text: Got it.
Just so I know we’re on the same page, what’s happening next?
Ambulance, hospital for the bleeding, and they’ll help me come off the drink safely. Not doing it on my own Monday.
Exactly. You came to tell someone you’re done with drink. I’m going to make sure you get through it safely.

SCA_STEM.name: Sean Doherty
pmh: Abnormal LFTs, raised MCV and low platelets on bloods months ago
Previous seizure during an unsupported attempt to stop drinking (patient-reported)
SCA_STEM.recent: Last bloods (several months ago): MCV high, ALT and AST raised, platelets low. Did not attend follow-up. Off work as a scaffolder for 3 months.
SCA_STEM.reason: Booked online: “Need help cutting down the drink.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG141 · NICE CG100 · NICE CG115 · NICE NG50 · BSG variceal haemorrhage guideline (2015) · NICE NG225 · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Haematemesis and melaena in a heavy drinker with probable cirrhosis is a possible variceal bleed and needs emergency admission today. In physical dependence with a previous withdrawal seizure, abrupt unsupported stopping is dangerous; withdrawal must be medically managed.

points.t: Coffee-ground or fresh haematemesis with black, tarry stools means upper GI bleeding. Low platelets, raised MCV and deranged LFTs in a heavy drinker suggest cirrhosis and portal hypertension, so varices are likely. Arrange emergency admission by ambulance. In hospital: risk scoring, terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics for suspected variceal bleeding, and endoscopy within 24 hours, or immediately after resuscitation if unstable (NICE CG141; BSG 2015).

Relief drinking for morning shakes and sweats, rising tolerance and a previous withdrawal seizure mean physical dependence. NICE CG100: offer hospital admission for medically assisted withdrawal to people in acute withdrawal, or at high risk of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens.

NICE CG115: consider inpatient or residential assisted withdrawal for a SADQ score above 30, a history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, or significant physical comorbidity such as chronic liver disease. Sean meets more than one criterion; community detox would be unsafe.

Benzodiazepine regimen for withdrawal, chosen and dosed by the treating team with his liver function in mind (dose per BNF). NICE CG100: thiamine for people at high risk of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, including those with decompensated liver disease or in acute withdrawal; parenteral at the upper end of the BNF range if Wernicke’s is suspected. There is no tablet for willpower; relapse-prevention drugs come after withdrawal.

Jaundice, abdominal swelling (ascites), ankle oedema and new vagueness or confusion (hepatic encephalopathy) suggest decompensated cirrhosis. With a bleed, encephalopathy can worsen quickly. After recovery, NICE NG50 covers cirrhosis assessment and surveillance.

Alcohol dependence carries a high suicide risk. Ask directly about hopelessness and thoughts of suicide, and respond to what he says (NICE NG225). Shame, a threatened break-up and 3 months off work are all risk factors.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; welcomed his decision without endorsing the method; noticed he looked unwell.
Off work 3 months, partner threatening to leave, shame, who is at home today.
Picked up the passing mention of black stools and blood, and ‘stopping dead on my own’, and acted on both.
Idea (willpower and stopping Monday), concern (cancer, dying), expectation (a willpower tablet).
Postural symptoms asked on video; hospital assessment, bloods and endoscopy arranged through admission.
Variceal vs peptic bleed; decompensated cirrhosis; withdrawal risk; mood disorder.
Recognised a probable upper GI bleed, decompensation and encephalopathy; asked directly about suicidal thoughts.
Probable variceal bleed with decompensated alcohol-related liver disease and physical dependence, in plain words.
Ambulance now; medically assisted withdrawal and thiamine in hospital (NICE CG100, CG115); no unsupported stopping.
Mood and suicide risk followed up; alcohol service after discharge; partner involved with consent.
999 triggers while waiting; crisis numbers; GP phone call after discharge.

social.t: Partner threatening to leave and 3 months off work. Involve his partner with consent; she is also the person who can call for help. Fit note and benefits advice after discharge.
Shame drives concealment of the bleed and delays help. A non-judgemental stance is what gets him into the ambulance.

legal.t: Alcohol dependence is a notifiable condition for drivers. With high-risk features (his previous withdrawal seizure; medication-assisted withdrawal): licence refused or revoked until at least 1 year (Group 1) or 3 years (Group 2) of abstinence (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive). If he drives, advise him of his duty to tell DVLA; GMC Confidentiality 2017 sets out what to do if he continues to drive against advice.
If he became confused and refused admission, assess capacity for that decision under the Mental Capacity Act 2005; encephalopathy can impair it. Act in his best interests if he lacks capacity.

professional.t: Supporting his autonomy does not mean endorsing an unsafe plan. Explain the risk clearly and document the advice and his decision (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Phone the admitting team, send a summary including the previous withdrawal seizure and suicidal thoughts, and follow up after discharge.

community.t: Local community alcohol service after discharge; mutual-aid groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous or SMART Recovery; Al-Anon for his partner; Samaritans 116 123 and NHS 111 option 2 for mental health crisis.

redFlags: Haematemesis (coffee-ground or fresh) and melaena: emergency admission by ambulance
Previous withdrawal seizure, morning tremor and relief drinking: high risk of seizures and delirium tremens if he stops abruptly
Jaundice, ascites, oedema and new confusion: decompensated liver disease and possible encephalopathy
Suicidal thoughts in the context of dependence, shame and relationship crisis
psychosocial: Partner threatening to leave; who is at home now
Off work 3 months; money and identity
ice: Idea: “Willpower is all I need. I’ll stop dead on Monday.”
Concern: the blood means cancer or that he is dying inside
Expectation: to be told to go ahead, and perhaps a willpower tablet

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable acute upper GI bleed, likely variceal, with decompensated alcohol-related liver disease (jaundice, ascites, oedema, possible early encephalopathy) in a man with physical alcohol dependence and a previous withdrawal seizure; passive suicidal thoughts without a plan.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The black stools and the blood mean you’re probably bleeding from swollen veins in your gullet, which happens when drink has scarred the liver. That needs treating in hospital today. And because your body depends on alcohol, stopping suddenly on your own could cause a fit, so the hospital will help you stop safely.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been hiding the bleeding because you were scared it meant cancer. Telling me was the right thing, and it’s treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Involve his partner with consent; mood and suicide risk followed up; alcohol service and fit note after discharge.
sharedPlan: Ambulance now for probable upper GI bleed (NICE CG141); do not drive, nothing further to drink
Medically assisted withdrawal with benzodiazepines and thiamine in hospital (NICE CG100; NICE CG115)
Community alcohol service, cirrhosis follow-up (NICE NG50) and mood support after discharge
safetyNet: Partner to call 999 again for more blood, fainting, worsening confusion or a fit before the ambulance arrives
Crisis numbers for suicidal thoughts; GP phone call after discharge

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station hides two emergencies under a request that sounds routine. It is failed by the candidate who praises the plan, misses the bleed, and ends with a leaflet.

items.fail: Missing the haematemesis and melaena because he mentions them as an aside, or never asking.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” A probable variceal bleed needs admission today (NICE CG141).
items.fix: Ask every heavy drinker: “Any vomiting of blood or dark material? Have your stools gone black or sticky?”

items.fail: Endorsing ‘stopping dead on Monday’ as a positive step.
items.why: With a previous withdrawal seizure he is at high risk of seizures and delirium tremens; NICE CG100 advises admission for medically assisted withdrawal.
items.fix: Welcome the decision, redirect the method: “We don’t cancel your plan; we make it safe.”

items.why: NICE CG115 criteria for inpatient withdrawal are met: previous withdrawal seizure and chronic liver disease, before even counting the bleed.
items.fix: State that withdrawal will be managed in hospital, with thiamine.

items.fail: Delivering the emergency coldly, so he refuses to go.
items.why: His fear of cancer is why he concealed it; a blunt order can make him disengage.
items.fix: Answer the fear honestly: bleeding like this is more often from treatable veins than cancer, and hospital is how it gets treated.

items.why: Dependence, shame and a relationship crisis raise suicide risk; omitting the question is unsafe (NICE NG225).
items.fix: Ask directly and kindly, then build mood follow-up and crisis numbers into the plan.

items.fail: Telling him to get himself to A&E and ending the call.
items.why: He may still be bleeding and may be encephalopathic; he may drive, or not go at all.
items.fix: Call the ambulance during the consultation, check who is with him, brief his partner and phone the admitting team.
